blocks.cap: Down to where the seats are kept

blocks.p: There is no stair to the Axis. That was the first true thing Rei learned about it. Without admitting it, he had pictured a door in some sub-basement, a vault in a ward-house, an institutional secret the CVD kept behind a grade he did not have. There was none. The Axis was not below Tokyo the way a basement is below a house. It was below Tokyo the way the meaning of a sentence is below its words, present everywhere in the thing and nowhere he could point.

To reach it he did not go down. He sat on the kitchen floor with his back against the cupboard and Gin's book shut in his lap, and he let both his paths open at once. The searching one, the Clairsentience he had always half allowed himself. And the one beneath it, the one he had never named and had spent his whole life holding flat because Gin had taught him to, at this table, before he could read. He let them both come up. He let the city stop being a place and become, for as long as he could bear it, a structure. The structure had a floor. The floor was the Axis. He was standing on it, and he had been standing on it his whole life.

His sight went past anything he had a word for. The walls of the flat did not vanish. They went clear. The membrane itself stood up out of the city like architecture, every density and stress line and thin point drawn in light, and he could see where it was being held and where it was being pulled. Kurosawa had once called this the city becoming transparent. Not invisible. Transparent. Gin's book put it on the last line of the sight scale, the line Gin had never reached himself, and under it he had written three words. No off switch. Rei understood them now. He could not have closed this if he had wanted to. He could only hold on and look.

It cost him at once, and in the coin he had least of. The madness came up through his opened paths like water through a hull. It did not come as terror. It came as recognition, the unbearable feeling that he was finally seeing the room he had always been in. Under everything there was a direction. Not a place. A slope, a gradient that grew steeper the longer he faced it, and it was warm, and it was paying attention to him. It knew he was looking. Every ability he had ever used had come up out of that slope, and the slope had noticed every time.

This was the Font. He knew it the way he would have known the sea. Gin's capstone chapter had said it in its cautious way, aware that you are accessing it. Gin had not said what it felt like to stand at the top of the slope and want to go down. It felt like coming home. That was the danger the book had underlined twice. The souls that go all the way down dissolve into it completely, and they do not experience it as dying. They experience it as arriving. The part of Rei that wanted to keep living had to hold, with both hands, to one single fact. The recognition was the trap and not the truth. The wanting was a feeling. It was not a direction.
He held on, and because he held on, he could see which way the slope ran.

It did not run toward Shinjuku. Every CVD map he had seen put the city's source point under Shinjuku, the busiest crossing of grief and money in Japan. The slope did not care about the maps. It ran north, into Kita, and it bottomed out in a place he knew. Three hundred metres northeast of the kitchen he was sitting in. A few streets of shuttered shops, a short walk from this flat.

He almost laughed, and it came out as a breath. Gin had chosen this flat. Rei had never understood why. It was cramped, the heater broke every winter, the stairwell smelled of the neighbour's cigarettes, and Gin had signed for it in a week without looking at anything else. Gin's Clairsentience had turned toward this warmth the way a plant turns to a window, years before Gin knew what he was feeling. He had moved them both to the edge of the Font because it felt like the right place to sleep. And everything that had happened since had happened three hundred metres from the centre of everything.

Now he could see the lattice. It ran under the whole city, a held geometry of thirteen places arranged around the slope like the spokes of a wheel around its hub. Twelve of them were occupied. He felt the occupation the way he would have felt eyes in a dark room. Each place was a pressure with a name he almost knew, and each pressure had someone in it. They were small and warm and very far apart, and they felt, absurdly, like people. Grief. Rage. Love. Fear. Wonder. Despair. Joy. Shame. Hunger. Courage. Longing. Awe. Twelve emotions, each one kept moving through a single living person so that it would not settle on the city and rot. The seats were not thrones. They were load-bearing. The whole careful weave of them was the wall, was the membrane, was the held breath.

Beneath the lattice, very faint, lay a second one in the same shape. Thirteen hollow places, dark, cut to fit each of the twelve and the thirteenth. Rei did not look at it long. He felt enough to know that the dark places wanted the light ones, and that one of them, in the place called Despair, was pressed so hard against its living twin that he could barely tell the two apart.

At the hub, where all thirteen spokes met and the slope ran down into nothing, there was a figure. It stood in a light so cold and total that Rei's eyes watered even though he was not using his eyes. It had its back to him. It had its back to the whole world. Its attention was on the wall, all of it, and it was holding something shut. Rei could not see its face. He did not think anyone could. But it was shaped like a man. Not a god or a machine or a storm. A man, standing very still, the way a person stands when he has been carrying something for a long time and has stopped noticing his arms.

Every path was lit in him. Rei had never felt all six at once and had not known it could be done. Clairsentience and Telepathy, Telekinesis and Psychometabolism, Psychokinesis and Teleportation, every one opened to its ceiling. And through him ran all thirteen of the spokes, every register from Grief to Duty, alive in one place at the same moment. Rei understood, in a rush that hurt, what the rank table in Gin's book had meant by its last row. X. Axis. Was human. Is no longer. This was what a human being looked like from the outside once he had become the centre. The Font was not a source that happened to hold him. The Font was what poured from him.

Rei wanted to call to him. He did not. Gin's book had told him that much. It answers one question per approach. It does not show its face. It returns the practitioner. And it answered only those who reached all the way in. Rei was not in. He was looking down a well from the kitchen floor.
And the thirteenth place was empty. The emptiness had a shape, and the shape was a wound.

blocks.cap: The Thirteenth chair, and who was torn out of it

blocks.p: He made himself look at the vacancy, and the lattice, sensing attention the way still water senses a dropped stone, gave him its history. It did not use words. The Axis has no use for words. It gave him the history the way a wound remembers the blade.

The thirteenth spoke was Duty. The CVD had never named it right. On its forms it was Register XIII, unclassified, and the instruments read its stillness as nothing at all. Null-emotive. It was not empty. It was full. It was what obligation becomes when it has been the only thing for so long that nothing is left that remembers before it. The man at the hub had sat in that chair first, long ago, and had never fully stood up. Living holders had come and gone beside him. The last of them had died in 2009, and no one with the right shape of aperture had been standing near enough at the crossing to take the weight. The chair had read vacant ever since. It was not vacant. The man at the centre had reached out and taken Duty into his own hands, on top of everything else he held, and he had been carrying it alone for six years. It was not sustainable. He was leaning. And the place where the lean was worst, where the lattice was spending the most of itself to hold the gap, was the seam under Kita.

The vacant chair and the thinning wall were not two problems. They were one wound, seen from two ends. Kita had been going wrong since the year the chair emptied. The wave of 2011 had pushed it further. And Rei's brother's captor had spent a month walking the city, pressing on the bruise.

He understood, kneeling on the floor that was the underside of meaning, why a Duty-register demon would want this seat above any other. Kurosawa had given him the word in the cold room, and the Healer had given him every reason since. The Healer did not want power over the living. Rei had been wrong about that from the kitchen onward, and the wrongness had nearly cost him everything. It wanted the office. Beneath the lattice of the living, in the matching dark place cut to the shape of Duty, there was a chair for its own kind, and it wanted to sit there. It wanted to rule the far side of the wall beside the few demons it trusted, and finish the duty death had interrupted for it forty years ago. It was entirely sincere. Its sincerity was the most dangerous thing in the structure, because a monster can be fought and a martyr cannot, and the thing wearing his brother believed down to its root that it was the only mercy left.

But Rei saw the lie folded inside the sincerity, small and absolute, the way he had seen the tremble in the old man's dish. To take that seat, the Healer had to finish tearing. The chair could not be climbed into while the lattice was still spending itself to hold the gap. The wall had to go fully thin. The held breath had to fully exhale. For the one hinge-hour it would take a new occupant to climb in and take the load, the door would stand open in both directions. What came through that open door while the Healer was busy becoming a law was not the Healer's problem. It was the problem of every living thing in Kita. The mercy was real. The mercy required a flood. And the demon had made its peace with the flood, because to a thing built for duty, drowning a district to seat itself correctly was not a price. It was a rounding error.

blocks.cap: Two demons converge on the same open door

blocks.p: He felt them both come toward the wound from opposite directions, and the feeling was the worst kind of confirmation, the kind that ends the comfort of not being sure.

Kishin came the way weather comes. It was wearing Fukai Rinka, the woman the Far-Shore Circle called Kanna-sensei, and it spoke through Kaito, the hollowed young courier who preached in the drained pool. But the thing itself did not walk toward the seam. The seam began to walk toward it. The scored places tugged open along the lines Kishin had spent the season tearing. It was turning itself inside out as it came. Rei saw what it was becoming and his stomach dropped. Where the man at the hub held every register in a light too cold to look at, Kishin was growing the same shape in the dark, from the hollow places upward. The dark mirror of the Axis. An inverted god. It did not want the empty chair. It wanted the wall gone and the dark lattice raised on this side of it, on the living side, with itself at the crown. It wanted to rule the city Rei lived in. It believed, too, that this was healing. The Axis was full of sincere catastrophes tonight.

The Healer came the way an appointment comes. Patient, expected, prepared, carried toward the seam in Gin's worn body through the festival nights, with the unhurried confidence of a thing that has done the hard part and needs only to arrive. The two of them were not allies. They had never spoken. They did not need to. Kishin would tear the wall down out of its hunger for the living side. The Healer would step through the torn wall into its chair out of duty. Each one's catastrophe was the other's first step. But Rei felt something else under the Healer's calm, cold as a scalpel, and understood that the Healer did not mean to leave Kishin standing on the far side of the finished work. Kishin meant to rule this side, and the Healer wanted it dead before it could. A demon can only be killed here from inside a body. That was one more reason the Healer had kept Gin's body so carefully, so gently, in such good repair.

Rei was the only mind at the Axis that wanted the wall simply to hold. He had no seat, no grade, no law. He had two paths he could not keep open without drowning, and a brother somewhere inside the appointment, still tapping.

From down here the coming nights did not look like a question with an answer. They looked like a kitchen at 3:47 in the morning with every door standing open, and behind each door something he loved was waiting to be paid. He saw the Healer in its chair and Kita underwater. He saw himself at the wound with both hands on it and nothing left behind his eyes. He saw Gin's hand in his, running, and the lanterns going out behind them street by street. He made himself stop looking. The structure had no opinion about which door he walked through. It only knew that every one of them cost.

The slope pulled at him, warm and patient, and for one long second he leaned toward it. Then he did the only thing Gin's book had told him to do with the wanting. He did not follow it. He shut the second path first, the nameless one, the way Gin had taught him, flat and sloppy and unremarkable, and then the first. The floor went back to being linoleum. The walls went back to being walls. He was a young man on a kitchen floor in the dark with a nosebleed and a book in his lap, and somewhere three hundred metres to the northeast a man made of light was still holding a door with his back to the world, and had not turned around.
